title: Why Can Some Insects Walk on Water, According to Science Today?
parts: That insect is not really floating. It is standing on tiny dents in the water.
Its legs touch the pond, and the water pushes back.
So why can some insects walk on water?
One familiar case is the water strider. Wikipedia says these insects generally live on the surface of calm waters.
Most species are between two and twelve millimeters long. Wikipedia adds that most live in fresh water, though about ten percent are marine.
Their secret starts with water itself. Wikipedia says a molecule at the surface is pulled inward, because it has neighbors on fewer sides.
The result, it says, is that the surface behaves like an elastic film.
Our comparison: a stretched sheet of fabric. Press gently, and it dents instead of breaking.
Wikipedia says a strider's feet make dents in the surface, and the surface tension pushes back.
But the legs matter too. Wikipedia says they are long, slender, and hydrophobic, which means they repel water.
It adds that long, slender legs spread the body's weight over a large area.
Wikipedia says the body is covered in microhairs that repel water, several thousand per square millimeter.
If an insect is pushed under, those hairs trap air, which helps it stay afloat and gives it air to breathe.
MIT News says climbing back out of the water takes a force akin to lifting a hundred times a strider's body weight.
In twenty fifteen, a study reported by a science news site examined strider legs closely. It found tapered hairs with tiny grooves.
It reported that tiny droplets that condense on the hairs get pushed off without any outside force.
Standing is one thing. Moving is another.
Wikipedia says the middle legs are longest, an adaptation for propulsion, and the hind legs steer.
Discover magazine says the dip in the surface, called a meniscus, acts like an oar.
In two thousand three, MIT News reported that the main push comes from small swirls under the surface, called vortices.
It said the little waves the legs make do not play a significant role. Wikipedia describes it differently: a circular surface wave whose crest gives thrust.
MIT News adds that researchers also built a small robot that pushes off the same way.
Wikipedia says striders often move at one meter per second or faster.
Wikipedia adds that they also use their front legs to feel ripples from struggling prey.
Here is our reading. It is a team effort: surface tension, light bodies, dry legs, and clever rowing.
Size has a limit. MIT News says a giant strider, about twenty centimeters long, is the largest that can still walk on water.
Next time you see a pond, look closely. In the right light, you may spot tiny dimples under each foot.
Now picture that pond from a window, as a storm rolls in. A flash lights up the water.
Then, seconds later, thunder. Why does the sound come late?
